title: Engineering Production Handbook
content:
Engineering Production Handbook

Release Preparation
Production changes should begin with a clearly defined scope and expected outcome. Engineers should understand which services, dependencies, customers, and operational workflows may be affected. Changes should be small enough to reason about and should avoid combining unrelated behavior into a single release. High-risk changes should identify owners responsible for monitoring the rollout and responding to unexpected behavior.

CI Validation
Before a production change is merged, the required continuous integration checks must pass. These checks may include unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, security scanning, formatting validation, and build verification. A failing required check should not be bypassed simply to accelerate a release. Intermittent failures should be investigated rather than repeatedly retried until they pass.

Feature Flags
Changes that introduce significant behavioral differences should use feature flags when practical. A feature flag allows functionality to be enabled gradually without requiring another deployment. Flags should have a documented owner and expected removal date. Teams should avoid leaving obsolete flags permanently in the codebase because they increase complexity and make system behavior harder to reason about.

Database Migrations
Database changes should preserve compatibility between application versions during a rollout. Prefer additive schema changes before destructive changes. For example, introduce a new column before deploying code that depends on it, migrate data separately when necessary, and remove obsolete schema only after older application versions can no longer use it. A destructive migration can make application rollback impossible even when the previous application artifact remains available.

Progressive Rollout
Production releases should be exposed gradually when infrastructure supports progressive deployment. Begin with a limited percentage of traffic or a small set of instances and evaluate system health before increasing exposure. Large releases should avoid moving directly from zero exposure to the entire production environment when a safer staged rollout is available.

Health Validation
After deployment, engineers should verify application health rather than assuming a successful deployment command means a successful release. Validation should include relevant service metrics, error rates, latency, logs, dependency health, and important user workflows. Automated health checks should complement, not completely replace, engineering judgment for significant releases.

Rollback
Every production-impacting release should have a practical recovery strategy. When a release introduces significant errors or customer impact, stop further rollout and determine whether rollback is safer than forward remediation. Use the standard deployment pipeline for rollback whenever possible. Database compatibility must be considered because destructive migrations may prevent an older application version from functioning correctly.

Post-Deployment Monitoring
Engineers should continue monitoring a release after initial health checks succeed. Some failures appear only under sustained traffic, asynchronous workloads, or less common user behavior. Teams should watch relevant dashboards and alerts for an appropriate period based on the risk of the change and document unexpected behavior for follow-up.

title: Platform Architecture Guide
content:
Platform Architecture Guide

Service Layer
HTTP APIs are exposed through FastAPI services. Route handlers should remain thin and focus on request validation, authentication context, response formatting, and delegation. Business logic should live in service-layer components rather than accumulating inside route handlers. This separation improves testing and prevents transport concerns from becoming tightly coupled to domain behavior.

Persistent Data
PostgreSQL is the primary durable relational data store. Persistent application state that must survive process restarts should be stored in an appropriate durable system rather than local process memory. Database access should occur through clearly defined repository or data-access boundaries so persistence concerns remain separate from business logic.

Caching
Redis may be used for short-lived cached data, distributed coordination, rate-limiting state, and other workloads where temporary data can safely be reconstructed. Engineers should not treat cached data as the authoritative system of record. Cache expiration and invalidation behavior should be explicitly considered when designing features that depend on cached values.

Background Processing
Long-running or asynchronous work should not block HTTP request handlers. Tasks such as large data processing operations, external synchronization, batch work, and expensive asynchronous workflows should be submitted to background workers. Request handlers should return an appropriate acknowledgement or job identifier when the caller does not need to wait for the work to complete.

External Providers
External services should be accessed through provider abstractions instead of being called directly throughout application code. Provider boundaries make retries, timeouts, authentication, observability, testing, and vendor replacement easier to manage. Route handlers should not directly call external AI models. They should delegate through the service layer and an AI provider abstraction.

Failure Boundaries
Network calls can fail, time out, or return malformed responses. Services should establish explicit timeout behavior and avoid assuming dependencies are always available. Retries should be limited to operations that are safe to repeat. Critical dependencies should expose useful health and operational signals so failures can be diagnosed without relying on guesswork.

Configuration
Environment-specific configuration should be injected through configuration management and environment variables rather than hard-coded into application modules. Secrets must not be committed to source control. Applications should fail clearly during startup when mandatory configuration is unavailable.

title: Reliability and Incident Response Handbook
content:
Reliability and Incident Response Handbook

Detection
Production incidents may be detected through automated alerts, customer reports, support escalation, or engineer observation. Alerts should identify actionable symptoms and provide enough context for the responding engineer to begin investigation. Monitoring systems should avoid creating excessive low-value alerts that train responders to ignore notifications.

Initial Response
When a production problem affects customers, notify the designated incident communication channel and establish ownership of the response. Identify an incident lead for significant events. Document the known impact and communicate verified information. The first objective is to reduce customer impact and restore healthy service, not to immediately explain every underlying cause.

Mitigation
Responders should evaluate the fastest safe path to reducing impact. Mitigation may include rollback, disabling a feature, shifting traffic, restarting unhealthy components, reducing load, or applying another understood operational procedure. Teams should distinguish mitigation from root-cause resolution. A temporary mitigation may restore service while deeper investigation continues later.

Escalation
On-call engineers should escalate when the incident requires expertise, permissions, authority, or system knowledge they do not have. Escalation is not a failure of the responder. Effective incident management brings the appropriate people into the response early enough to reduce impact. Ownership should remain clear as additional responders join.

Communication
Incident communication should focus on verified facts, current customer impact, actions underway, and the next expected update. Avoid speculation presented as fact. Significant incidents should maintain a timeline of important observations and actions so responders and stakeholders can understand how the event developed.

Root-Cause Analysis
Detailed root-cause investigation generally follows stabilization of the service. Responders should preserve useful evidence during mitigation, but service restoration takes priority during active customer impact. Root-cause analysis should examine technical causes as well as contributing process, monitoring, testing, and organizational factors.

Post-Incident Follow-Up
Significant incidents should produce concrete follow-up work. Actions may improve monitoring, automation, testing, documentation, architecture, operational procedures, or ownership. Follow-up items should have owners and should address meaningful contributors rather than merely documenting that an incident occurred.

title: Engineering Quality Guide
content:
Engineering Quality Guide

Pull Requests
A pull request should explain the problem being solved, the implementation approach, relevant test coverage, operational risk, and recovery strategy. The description should provide enough context for a reviewer to understand why the change exists without reconstructing the author's reasoning from the code alone.

Review
Reviewers should evaluate correctness, maintainability, security, observability, test coverage, operational risk, and scope. Approval should not mean only that the code appears to compile. Reviewers should consider how the change behaves in production, how failures will be detected, and whether future engineers will be able to understand and modify the implementation safely.

Testing
Unit tests should validate focused behavior and important edge cases. Integration tests should validate interactions between meaningful system boundaries. End-to-end tests should be reserved for critical workflows where validating the complete path provides sufficient value to justify their additional maintenance cost. Tests should provide confidence rather than simply increase coverage percentages.

Test Failures
A failing test should be investigated. Repeatedly rerunning a flaky test until it passes hides reliability problems in the test suite. Flaky tests reduce trust in CI and can cause engineers to ignore failures that represent real defects. Teams should repair, quarantine, or replace unreliable tests according to established engineering practices.

Observability
Production systems should expose enough telemetry to answer whether the service is healthy and why it is unhealthy. Useful signals commonly include latency, traffic, error rates, resource saturation, structured logs, traces, and domain-specific metrics. New critical workflows should include observability as part of implementation rather than adding it only after an incident occurs.

Logging
Logs should provide useful diagnostic context without exposing secrets or unnecessary sensitive data. Prefer structured logging with stable fields that can be searched and aggregated. Avoid high-volume logs that provide little operational value. Error logs should help responders understand what failed and provide identifiers necessary to correlate related events.

Maintainability
Code should optimize for clarity and safe modification rather than unnecessary abstraction. Shared abstractions should represent genuinely shared concepts. Engineers should avoid introducing generalized frameworks for hypothetical future requirements when a simpler implementation satisfies the current need.

title: AI Engineering Standards
content:
AI Engineering Standards

Provider Abstraction
Applications should access external AI models through a provider interface rather than calling a vendor SDK throughout the codebase. Provider abstractions centralize authentication, model selection, timeout behavior, retries, logging, and vendor-specific translation. This boundary also makes model providers easier to replace or compare.

Prompt Management
Prompts used by production workflows should be treated as application artifacts. Important prompts should be versioned, reviewed, and tested. Large prompts duplicated across application modules become difficult to maintain. Prompt changes can alter system behavior even when conventional application code remains unchanged.

Structured Outputs
When downstream application logic depends on model output, prefer explicit structured output contracts over parsing arbitrary prose. Validate model responses before using them in business logic. Applications should handle missing fields, malformed responses, and provider errors rather than assuming every model response satisfies the requested format.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Systems that answer questions using internal knowledge should retrieve relevant evidence before generation when model training data cannot be trusted to contain the required information. Retrieval systems should be evaluated separately from generation so teams can distinguish failures caused by missing evidence from failures caused by answer synthesis.

Cost Management
AI workloads should track model usage and avoid sending unnecessary context. Larger prompts and repeated model calls can increase cost and latency. Teams should choose models based on the quality required by the workflow rather than assuming the largest available model is necessary for every operation.

Reliability
External model APIs should be treated as network dependencies. Applications should define timeouts, error handling, and appropriate retry behavior. Workflows should consider what happens when the provider is unavailable, slow, rate-limited, or returns an unusable response.

Evaluation
Production AI systems should use repeatable evaluation datasets for important workflows. Evaluation should measure behavior that matters to users and should include realistic paraphrases, edge cases, and difficult examples. Architecture changes should be compared against a stable baseline rather than judged only from a handful of manually selected demonstrations.
